capex_program_basis: SpaceX-stated total Falcon 9 v1.0 development cost, independently verified by NASA. NASA also cites $390M including ~$90M of Falcon 1 heritage work. NASA COTS Space Act Agreement funding ($278M at 2006 signing, rising to $396M by 2011) is NASA's contribution only (bundled with Dragon demo flights), not SpaceX's total spend -- not directly comparable.
capex_first_launch_basis: No source isolates development cost incurred only through the first flight (June 2010) separately from the cumulative ~$300M figure reported in 2011.
payload_leo_note: Rated capacity, 200km circular/28.5 deg, Cape Canaveral, Falcon 9 Block 2 config (flew as v1.0), fully expendable. Actual v1.0 missions (Dragon) carried far less.
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: price / rated LEO capacity
notes: NASA's NAFCOM cost model separately estimated Falcon 9 would have cost NASA $3.977B (FY2010$, NASA-culture cost-plus inputs) or $1.695B (commercial-culture inputs) if developed in-house -- a hypothetical counterfactual, not actual SpaceX spend, but the source of the famous 4-11x 'commercial vs cost-plus' comparison. No marginal/incremental production-cost figure (distinct from customer price) is publicly available for this version.

capex_program_basis: ESTIMATE (Payload Research, secondary analyst analysis): cumulative Falcon-family development cost through reusable Falcon 9 (Falcon 1 heritage + F9 expendable + reusability R&D); ~$1.9B if inflation-adjusted to 2024$. Not an official SpaceX total. Cross-check: Musk stated in March 2017 SpaceX had spent 'over $1 billion' self-funded on reusable-rocket technology specifically.
capex_first_launch_basis: NASA-verified total SpaceX development cost for Falcon 9 v1.0 + Falcon 1 heritage -- NOT Block-5-specific; no public figure isolates the incremental Block 5 (first flight May 2018) development cost alone. Included for completeness, but treat with caution as a 'cost to first launch' figure for THIS variant.
payload_leo_note: 22,800 kg expendable (no booster recovery) vs. ~17,400-18,500 kg with drone-ship/RTLS booster recovery (typical operational mode); reusable-mode figure varies by source/date due to Block 5 performance upgrades.
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: price / typical reusable-mode LEO capacity
notes: num_flights is total Falcon 9 launches across ALL variants (v1.0, v1.1/FT, Block 5) as of mid-2026; large majority since 2019 are Block 5. Annual cadence: 91 (2023), 132 (2024), 165 (2025), each a record. SpaceX exec Christopher Couluris separately stated marginal cost was '$28M with everything' in a 2020 briefing -- executive statements, not audited figures. NSSL government task orders run far higher (~$102-105M, FY2024/25 Phase 3 awards).

capex_program_basis: Elon Musk's stated total self-funded investment ('over half a billion dollars, or more'), given in post-launch remarks immediately after the Feb 2018 debut/IOC flight; no government funding; leveraged existing Falcon 9 tooling. Musk did not distinguish total-program cost from cost-to-first-launch, so the same figure is used for both bases here. ESTIMATE cross-check (Payload Research): FH-specific increment over reusable F9 of ~$500M (~$614M in 2024$).
capex_first_launch_basis: Same Musk quote, made immediately after the Feb 2018 demo flight; not separately verified from total program cost.
payload_leo_note: 63,800 kg fully expendable maximum; most flown missions instead recover the two side boosters with center core expended (~57,000 kg). The $97M list price historically applies to a partial-recovery flight, not the 63,800 kg expendable max, so this $/kg pairing understates true expendable cost-efficiency.
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: partial-recovery price / fully-expendable rated capacity (inconsistent basis, see note)
notes: Musk separately quoted ~$150M 'at most' for a fully-expendable flight (Feb 2018); on that internally-consistent basis, $/kg ~$2,350. NSSL/USSF contract prices run much higher and include non-recurring infrastructure (e.g. USSF-67 = $316M, includes pad/fairing/NRO-facility costs); NASA Psyche mission = $117M. No FH-specific marginal cost distinct from price was found. 100% mission success across 12 flights; cadence is low/irregular.

capex_program_basis: SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen's sworn court declaration (~May 19, 2023, ~1 month after IFT-1): SpaceX invested 'more than $3 billion' in Starbase facility + Starship/Super Heavy development, July 2014 through the filing date. Closest available cumulative actual-spend figure, but blends facility construction with vehicle R&D and slightly postdates IFT-1. Distinct from NASA's $2.89B HLS Option A contract (April 2021), which funds the lunar-lander work only, not SpaceX's total investment.
capex_first_launch_basis: SpaceX does not disclose a 'cost to IFT-1' figure separate from cumulative/annual R&D spend; no source cleanly isolates it.
payload_leo_note: SpaceX-cited expendable-configuration maximum (~250 t); reusable configuration cited as 100-150 t. Figures vary across SpaceX communications over time; treat as approximate/aspirational, not flight-proven.
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: ESTIMATE marginal cost / aspirational expendable capacity (highly speculative)
notes: ESTIMATES/TARGETS clearly flagged: Musk's oft-cited $2M (sometimes $1-3M) marginal-cost target is explicitly for a fully-reusable, high-cadence vehicle and does NOT apply to this analysis's expendable scope -- reported for context only, not used as a data point. The $100M/$400-per-kg figures are Payload Research analyst ESTIMATES (methodology not fully disclosed), dated ~2024, slightly after the IFT-1 window. No NASA OIG report independently estimates SpaceX's total Starship self-investment as of April 2023; a genuine, expected gap since SpaceX does not publish true costs. IFT-1 ended in vehicle loss via Flight Termination System ~4 min into flight; no payload deployed.

capex_program_basis: Orbital Sciences' own estimated total Antares/Cygnus development cost per SEC filings (up from $458M in Q4 2011), against NASA's COTS Space Act Agreement cash milestone payments of $288M (final value, up from $170M in 2008) -- NASA's contribution portion only. Antares rocket and Cygnus spacecraft development costs appear bundled together, not cleanly separable.
capex_first_launch_basis: Same $472M figure, reported ~1 year before the April 2013 debut flight -- best available proxy for cost incurred through first launch, though not an exact first-launch cutoff.
payload_leo_note: 8,000 kg rated LEO capacity, Antares 230/230+; actual average cargo delivered per Cygnus mission was only ~2,600 kg (Cygnus itself, not the rocket, is usually the limiting factor).
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: bundled NASA CRS service price / rated LEO capacity (NOT a pure launch-only price; no commercial launch market exists for Antares)
notes: opex_price_usd ($339M) is a fully-bundled NASA CRS-1 service price (launch + Cygnus spacecraft production + NASA program overhead), per Planetary Society's contract-data analysis -- 1.86x SpaceX Dragon's cost over the same contract period. Using actual delivered cargo (~2,600 kg) instead of rated capacity, $/kg would be ~$130,385/kg. 18 total orbital launches (17 success, 1 failure -- Oct 2014 Orb-3 pad explosion). 200-series (Russian RD-181 powered) retired Aug 2023 after post-invasion supply cutoff; Cygnus has since flown on Falcon 9. A new Antares 330 variant (Firefly-built first stage) targets NET 2026.

capex_program_basis: NASA's own end-of-program total life-cycle cost estimate, 1971-2011 (development + 135 flights + facilities). Alternate figures: $192B (2010$) actual spend 1971-2010 per economist Roger Pielke Jr.'s reconstruction; $254.521B (2024$) per a 2013 peer-reviewed AIAA/JSR retrospective, split $52.621B DDT&E + $201.9B operations & sustainment.
capex_first_launch_basis: DDT&E only, reconstructed from actual NASA budget-request obligations FY1972-1984 (Planetary Society); window runs a few years past the April 1981 first flight (STS-1) since that's how NASA's own R&D budget line closed out. $10.606B if facilities construction is added.
payload_leo_note: Max rated payload to ~204km/28.5 deg orbit; only 16,050 kg to the higher-inclination ISS orbit.
opex_per_kg_basis: fully-loaded average cost (2018$) / rated LEO capacity
notes: GAO's FY1993 marginal cost ($44.4M) covers only consumables/personnel that scale with flight rate, explicitly excluding ~90% of fixed institutional overhead. GAO's FY1993 'average cost per flight' was $413.5M then-year (still excludes ~$30.2B sunk development cost through 1992). NASA publicly cited ~$450M/mission (nominal, 2011) near program end. Independent fully-loaded estimate: ~$1.5B/flight (2010$) per Pielke. $61,720/kg uses the $1,697M (2018$) NASA-affiliated peer-reviewed figure; to ISS orbit (16,050kg) this becomes ~$105,800/kg. 2 losses: Challenger (1986), Columbia (2003).

capex_program_basis: Cumulative SLS-rocket-only obligations since program inception (~2011) through first flight (Nov 2022). Combined with Orion ($20.4B) and Exploration Ground Systems ($5.7B), total Artemis vehicle-side cost through 2022 was $49.9B. No single authoritative updated total-to-date (mid-2026) figure was found.
capex_first_launch_basis: NASA's own official development cost to reach initial SLS capability (Artemis I): $2.7B formulation/design + $9.1B development, per GAO reporting. Narrower scope than the $23.8B total-obligations figure (excludes production/launch-support infrastructure spend).
payload_leo_note: SLS Block 1 configuration; NASA typically quotes Trans-Lunar Injection mass (>27t) instead since all SLS missions target the Moon, not LEO.
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: fully-loaded avg cost (SLS+Orion+ESM+EGS) / Block 1 LEO capacity
notes: $2.2B = SLS-only production cost (NASA OIG, marginal proxy); $4.1B = SLS+Orion+European Service Module+Exploration Ground Systems combined average for Artemis I-IV, which OIG called 'unsustainable.' GAO-23-105609 (2023) found NASA does not track per-mission production costs transparently. Artemis II (crewed lunar flyby) launched April 1, 2026 and returned April 10-11, 2026.

capex_program_basis: Total program cost (development + production of ~15 vehicles), Saturn V specifically, reconstructed from NASA Historical Reference Collection budget documents (peer-reviewed, Space Policy journal); ~$80B in 2025 dollars. Alternate figure: $6.417B (1964-1973 nominal appropriations) per NASA/Wikipedia budget records. Total Saturn family (V + IB + I + engines) = $9.4B.
capex_first_launch_basis: No isolated figure found; all sources report a combined development+production total spanning all ~15 vehicles (1961-1973) rather than separating cost through the first launch (Apollo 4, Nov 1967) alone.
payload_leo_note: Uprated Block II configuration (Apollo 15-17 / Skylab); earlier vehicles rated ~118,000 kg.
opex_per_kg_basis: fully-loaded per-launch cost (2018$) / uprated LEO capacity
notes: No formal marginal-vs-fully-loaded split exists in the literature; each vehicle was built to a fixed government contract, not mass-produced. The standard figure is $185M (1969$, the Saturn V's notional share of Apollo 11's $355M total mission cost); a 2018 NASA-affiliated peer-reviewed paper inflation-adjusts this to $728M (2018$), used here for consistency with the Shuttle/Titan IV/Titan II $/kg figures from the same source. Total Apollo program cost (spacecraft+launch vehicles+facilities) was $25.4-25.8B then-year (~$309B in 2025$).

capex_program_basis: Air Force's December 1990 Selected Acquisition Report ESTIMATE for total program acquisition cost (65-66 vehicles over 16 years), reported via GAO. This is a program cost estimate, not a closed-out actual-cost figure.
capex_first_launch_basis: No isolated DDT&E-only figure found separate from the total procurement-program estimate above.
payload_leo_note: Titan IV-B configuration; earlier IV-A slightly lower.
opex_per_kg_basis: NASA-affiliated peer-reviewed inflation-adjusted (2018$, basis year 1989) per-launch cost / rated LEO capacity
notes: Marginal/fully-loaded figures are from the 1997 NASA Cassini/Titan-IV-Centaur launch (GAO NSIAD-95-141BR): $253.4M = direct NASA payment to Air Force for booster+Centaur+launch services; $451.7M = total NASA-side mission cost including integration contract and reserves (this specific NASA/Centaur configuration is somewhat pricier than a bare USAF Titan IV-B). A widely repeated $432M figure (dollar-year unclear) traces only to a secondary Astronautix essay, not a primary government document. Retired 2005 (high cost, toxic hypergolic propellants), replaced by EELV (Atlas V/Delta IV). 22 Titan IV-A + 17 Titan IV-B launches.

capex_program_basis: TOTAL Project Gemini program cost (spacecraft $797.4M + launch vehicles $409.8M + support $76.2M), per a Jan. 1969 NASA report to Congress. The $409.8M 'launch vehicles' line combines Titan II GLV boosters AND Atlas-Agena target vehicles; cannot be isolated further in the public accounting found -- treat this as whole-program, not launch-vehicle-only.
capex_first_launch_basis: Titan-II-specific (non-Agena) cost line item, revised as of May 1962 (nearly 2 years before the April 1964 first launch), up from an original $113.0M estimate. This is the only vehicle-specific figure found, though it is a pre-launch program ESTIMATE, not a final actual cost.
payload_leo_note: Gemini spacecraft mass to LEO.
opex_per_kg_basis: NASA-affiliated peer-reviewed inflation-adjusted (2018$, basis year 1962) per-launch cost / capsule mass -- likely reflects the generic Titan II space-launcher config rather than the specifically man-rated GLV variant; treat with caution
notes: NO reliable vehicle-specific marginal or fully-loaded per-launch figure exists in public sources for the Titan II GLV alone. The only per-flight economics available is a WHOLE-PROGRAM figure (booster+spacecraft combined, not launch-vehicle-only): ~$723M/crewed flight (2010$) across 10 crewed missions, from Claude Lafleur's widely cited Space Review cost-comparison analysis -- NOT used as this row's opex figure since it isn't launch-vehicle-only. Derived from the LGM-25C Titan II ICBM; man-rating added a Malfunction Detection System, redundancy, radio guidance, and a pogo-oscillation fix. First crewed flight (Gemini 3): 1965-03-23. Last flight (Gemini 12): 1966-11-11. 12/12 successful.

capex_program_basis: Full Atlas ICBM crash-program cost: missile R&D, production of ~350 missiles, and construction of 129 launch complexes (e.g. Vandenberg). Roughly one-fourth (~$2B) went to design/development, the remainder to production and launch-complex construction. Eisenhower-era, highest-national-priority Cold War program (comparable in scale to the Manhattan Project, ~$2B).
capex_first_launch_basis: No figure isolating R&D cost through first flight (June 1957) exists separately from the whole-program total; only the rough ~$2B 'design and development' quarter-share of the $8B total is available, and it spans the full multi-year program through 1959 operational deployment, not just to first launch.
payload_leo_note: Atlas LV-3B / Atlas D configuration used for Mercury-Atlas; payload figure is the Mercury capsule mass to LEO.
opex_per_kg_basis: LOW CONFIDENCE: unit price / capsule mass, secondary enthusiast source only
notes: LOW-CONFIDENCE FIGURES FLAGGED: the $3.5M early estimate and $8.309M (1965$) unit-price figures trace only to Encyclopedia Astronautica/astronautix.com, a secondary enthusiast reference that could not be independently re-verified during this research (site returned HTTP 503) -- treat as indicative only. NASA's Project Mercury (Redstone + Atlas flights combined) cost $384.1M total (1963 accounting); the $82.9M 'launch vehicles' budget line spans ~20 missions across BOTH booster types and cannot be isolated to per-Atlas-launch cost. Flight count of 24 is an approximate tally of Atlas A/B/C/D orbital-relevant test and Mercury flights (350 missiles were built across the full SM-65 family, mostly as operational ICBMs never launched).

capex_program_basis: Combined EELV program (Atlas V + Delta IV together) total cost estimate, FY1998-2030, covering R&D, procurement, and launch services -- NOT broken out by vehicle in any public GAO reporting found. An earlier GAO estimate put total EELV investment at ~$8.2B through FY2008 alone.
capex_first_launch_basis: No Atlas-V-specific R&D-to-first-launch (Aug 2002) figure found; only combined EELV concept-definition contracts exist ($30M x4 in 1995, $60M x2 in 1996, $500M x2 'other transaction agreements' in 1998), none isolated to Atlas V alone.
payload_leo_note: Atlas V 401 configuration (4m fairing, no SRBs, single-engine Centaur) to LEO (185km, 28.5 deg); other configs range 8,210-18,850 kg.
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: 401-config list price / 401-config LEO capacity
notes: Other observed government contract prices: $187M (2010 NASA MAVEN), $164M (2013 USAF block buy, 401 config), $132.4M (2015 NASA TDRS-M), $153M (2016 list price, 551 config). Production ended 2024; no new sales since Aug 2021; being retired in favor of Vulcan Centaur (first flew Jan 2024). ~100-109 launches depending on tally date (100 confirmed as of June 2024; ~7-9 remained in the manifest as of April-May 2026, mostly Boeing Starliner and Amazon Leo/Kuiper missions).

capex_program_basis: Combined EELV program (Atlas V + Delta IV together) total cost estimate, FY1998-2030 -- the same program-wide figure as Atlas V; not broken out by vehicle in public GAO reporting.
capex_first_launch_basis: No Delta-IV-specific R&D-to-first-launch (Nov 2002) figure found; only combined EELV concept-definition contracts exist, not vehicle-isolated.
payload_leo_note: Delta IV Heavy to LEO (200km circular, 28.7 deg); Delta IV Medium (post RS-68A upgrade) payload to LEO is a much lower ~8,510 kg -- a separate figure, not used here.
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: Heavy 'standard' price / Heavy LEO capacity
notes: Price citations vary widely by year/contract: generic $164M+ figure (unclear year/source), $350M 'standard' per ULA CEO Tory Bruno (2018), up to $440M for NRO missions, $389.1M (2015 NASA Parker Solar Probe contract), and an unspecified price below $300M per a 2018 SpaceNews industry source ('the real price is a secret'). A $1.18B five-year NRO operations-support contract modification (2019) and a $149M single-mission task order also exist but bundle production/ops support, not a clean marginal per-launch cost. 45 total Delta IV family flights (Medium+Heavy); Delta IV Heavy alone flew 16 (15 success, 1 partial failure on its 2004 maiden flight). Last Medium flight Aug 2019; last (final) Heavy flight April 2024 (NROL-70), retired in favor of Vulcan Centaur.

capex_program_basis: Company-projected cumulative R&D + capex through end of 2025, per Rocket Lab CFO Adam Spice on an earnings call; revised up from an original $250-300M estimate given at/around the 2022 Investor Day, due to schedule delays. ALL FIGURES ARE COMPANY-DISCLOSED PROJECTIONS, NOT AUDITED FINAL COSTS, since Neutron has not yet flown.
capex_first_launch_basis: Same $360M figure serves as both program-to-date and cost-to-first-launch proxy since Neutron had not flown as of mid-2026 (first launch targeted Q4 2026 NET, already delayed from earlier targets); the two bases are not yet distinguishable.
payload_leo_note: Partially reusable configuration (first stage lands downrange); 15,000 kg if fully expendable, 8,500 kg if first stage returns to launch site. From Rocket Lab's Payload User's Guide.
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: predicted target price / predicted reusable-mode LEO capacity
notes: ALL FIGURES ARE PRE-FLIGHT PREDICTIONS/COMPANY PROJECTIONS, not flight-proven costs. Price range has also been reported more recently as $50-55M in secondary sources. Rocket Lab has signed Neutron launch contracts (Nov 2024 two-launch deal; May 2026 eight-launch bundled Neutron+Electron deal, the largest in company history) but has not disclosed per-launch pricing for these deals. All cost figures are company self-reported via earnings calls/investor days, not independently audited.

capex_program_basis: Official Blue Origin figure (Jeff Bezos statement, April 2017), likely stale/understated given years of subsequent delays and cost growth; reiterated as still current as of Jan 2025 launch by some reporting. THIRD-PARTY ESTIMATES ARE MUCH HIGHER (see notes) and are explicitly not confirmed by Blue Origin.
capex_first_launch_basis: No figure distinguishing cost-to-first-launch (Jan 2025) from total cumulative spend was found; Blue Origin does not disclose a breakdown.
payload_leo_note: Operational New Glenn 7x2 configuration to LEO; a future 9x4 configuration is claimed to exceed 70,000 kg but is not yet flying.
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: low end of commercial-price estimate range / rated LEO capacity
notes: THIRD-PARTY DEVELOPMENT-COST ESTIMATES (not confirmed by Blue Origin): ~$10B per an anonymous former Blue Origin employee (Forbes, Jan 2025); ~$14B per Space Capital investor Chad Anderson -- but that figure is for ALL of Blue Origin's cumulative spending, not New Glenn specifically. Blue Origin separately spent >$1B rebuilding Launch Complex 36 (completed 2021) and received ~$500M in USAF/Space Force NSSL Phase 2 cost-share funding post-2019. Commercial price estimates range $68-110M (analyst estimates; no official Blue Origin list price). NASA's ESCAPADE mission (NG-2) was priced at only ~$20M under NASA's VADR program -- an atypical discount since Blue Origin wanted to fly the mission anyway, not representative pricing. USSF NSSL Phase 3 Lane 2 (April 2025): ~7 flights for $2.4B total (~$343M/mission avg) -- a national-security mission-assurance price. Flight history: NG-1 (Jan 2025, success, booster landing failed), NG-2 (Nov 2025, success, first successful booster landing), NG-3 (April 2026, upper-stage malfunction stranded payload, though reused booster landed -- first New Glenn booster reuse). May 28 2026: a New Glenn first stage exploded during a pre-launch static-fire test, damaging the pad; return-to-flight expected before end of 2026.

capex_program_basis: No reliable public total-program or to-first-launch cost figure exists in dollar or even ruble terms. Original R-7/Soyuz-era development (1950s-60s, Korolev's OKB-1) was never disclosed with an auditable budget, and Soviet-era ruble accounting under a non-convertible currency makes any dollar conversion methodologically suspect. A genuine, expected data gap for a Soviet-origin vehicle.
capex_first_launch_basis: Same gap as total program cost; no isolating figure exists.
payload_leo_note: Soyuz-2.1b from Baikonur; secondary-source figure, varies 7,000-8,700 kg across sources/sites/variants -- the Soyuz family lacks one authoritative LEO number.
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: commercial price incl. Fregat upper stage / Soyuz-2.1b LEO capacity
notes: Commercial price is from Glavkosmos Launch Services (Roscosmos's commercial arm), stated at the 2018 International Astronautical Congress: $48.5M with Fregat upper stage, $35M without. Earlier Starsem-era commercial pricing (late 1990s-2000s) ran $35-52M. Flight count is inconsistent between sources: Wikipedia's variant table sums to ~1,100+ Soyuz-designated launches, while prose text cites 'more than 1,700 flights' for the broader Soyuz lineage -- reflects genuinely poor consolidated bookkeeping for this family, not a research omission.

capex_program_basis: No reliable dollar figure for the original Soviet UR-500/Proton development program (Chelomei design bureau, first flight 1965) exists publicly. Astronautix cites ~100 million rubles per launch as an internal Soviet OPERATING-cost figure (not development capex, and not reliably convertible to dollars given the non-convertible Soviet-era ruble) -- reported for context only, not used as a data point.
capex_first_launch_basis: Same gap as total program cost.
payload_leo_note: 180km circular orbit, 51.5 deg inclination, Baikonur (Proton-M).
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: commercial ILS price / Proton-M LEO capacity
notes: Commercial (International Launch Services) price trajectory: ~$28-35M (late 1990s) -> ~$65-85M (2000s) -> $95M (2014) reduced to $69-70M (April 2015) per Roscosmos chief Igor Komarov. Current Wikipedia infobox cites $65M. Roscosmos (Dmitry Rogozin) later stated an ambition to match Falcon 9 pricing, without a further specific figure. Flight count (431) is for the entire Proton/UR-500 family since 1965 (Proton-M alone: 116 launches as of Feb 2026, 105 successful).

capex_program_basis: RAND Corporation's 2005 policy report: Japan invested 'over 320 billion yen' in the combined H-2 and H-2A launcher development through spring 2004 (~$2.9B nominal at ~110 JPY/USD, 2004 basis). Combined-family figure, matching how this dataset groups H-II and H-IIA together.
capex_first_launch_basis: Not separately broken out from the combined H-II+H-IIA total above. Predecessor H-II alone reportedly had per-launch OPERATING costs of 14-19.5 billion yen (~$190M) -- an opex, not capex, figure, and a major driver for developing the cheaper H-IIA.
payload_leo_note: Range 10,000-15,000 kg depending on configuration (202/204); midpoint used for the $/kg calc.
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: commercial price / midpoint LEO capacity
notes: 49 of 50 H-IIA launches successful (98%), including a streak of 44 consecutive successes 2003-2025. Operated by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries under JAXA oversight since 2007. Final flight (GOSAT-GW) 28 June 2025.

capex_program_basis: No separate total-to-date figure found beyond the near-first-launch development cost below.
capex_first_launch_basis: ~200 billion yen development cost, per Spaceflight Now trade-press reporting around the time of the first (failed) launch attempt, Feb/March 2023 -- the best-documented, most consistently repeated figure for H3. Reported essentially at first-flight time, so likely functions as both total-program and to-first-launch cost; later fixes and the H3-30 variant's development are not separately broken out.
payload_leo_note: H3-24 (2-SRB) config to ISS-type orbit (420km, 51.64 deg) -- NOTE: a DIFFERENT configuration than the one the ~$34-51M price applies to (H3-30, no-SRB, ~4,000 kg to SSO). This mismatch means $/kg cannot be honestly computed across configs; left blank rather than blended.
opex_per_kg_basis: not computed: price and payload figures apply to different configurations (see payload_leo_note)
notes: MHI's stated target price is ~JPY5 billion for the H3-30 (lightest, no-SRB) configuration -- roughly half an H-IIA flight. Reported dollar values range $33-51M depending on source/year and yen exchange rate used ($33.9M per Wikipedia at 2024 rates, $33M per Reuters/Al Jazeera wire coverage, $50M per Spaceflight Now 2023). Record: F1 failed (7 Mar 2023, 2nd-stage ignition failure), 5 straight successes, F8 failed (22 Dec 2025, payload-adapter delamination destroyed QZS-5), F9 succeeded (12 June 2026, first H3-30 flight, return-to-flight). Net: 9 launches, 7 successes, 2 failures as of mid-2026.

capex_program_basis: No reliable original PSLV development-cost figure (1980s program through first 1993 flight) could be located in Wikipedia, ISRO's own site, or any Lok Sabha reply found -- a genuine gap. The oft-cited Rs 6,131 crore (2018 Cabinet approval, ~$750M 2023 basis) is a bulk-procurement/OPERATIONS budget for 30 flights 2019-2024, not development capex, and is deliberately excluded from this field.
capex_first_launch_basis: Same gap as total program cost.
payload_leo_note: PSLV-XL to 200km LEO at 30 deg inclination; ISRO's own site instead emphasizes 1,750 kg to 600km SSO, which is PSLV's more typical actual mission profile. Both reported since they are not interchangeable.
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: commercial price / PSLV-XL rated LEO capacity
notes: Marginal-cost proxy is NSIL's $104M contract for 5 industry-built PSLV-XL rockets (~$20.8M/unit). Commercial price range across sources is $15-31M depending on mission/payload; a single PSLV-C37 104-satellite rideshare was reported at ~$15M. Two consecutive failures (PSLV-C61, May 2025; PSLV-C62, Jan 2026) linked to third-stage anomalies prompted an ISRO expert review. 64 flights as of Jan 2026 (58 success, 4 failure, 1 partial failure, 1 pending classification).

capex_program_basis: No development-cost figure could be independently verified against a reliable primary or trade-press source; a commonly circulated '$500M' figure could not be confirmed against any cited reference and is therefore excluded rather than reported. What IS documented is production/procurement (not R&D) batch approvals: Rs 945 crore (April 2003, vehicles F01-F03 + long-lead items) and Rs 1,325 crore (Dec 2006, F04-F10).
capex_first_launch_basis: Same gap as total program cost.
payload_leo_note: LEO capacity; GTO capacity is a separate and lower 2,500 kg, SSO 3,000 kg -- GSLV's typical actual missions are GTO, not LEO.
opex_per_kg_basis: derived: commercial price / rated LEO capacity

notes: REAL, FLIGHT-PROVEN DATA (opex); capex_program genuinely undisclosed. opex_price of $168.5M is derived from a REAL, disclosed $337M FY2022 NSSL Phase 2 task order covering 2 missions (USSF-51 + USSF-106), announced Aug 2020 -- a blended Atlas V/Vulcan-era task order (USSF-51 ultimately flew on Atlas V; USSF-106 became Vulcan's first NSSL flight, Aug 2025), so treat as a real contract-derived proxy rather than a confirmed single-mission Vulcan-only price. NSSL Phase 3 Lane 2 (Apr 2025) separately gave ULA a ~$5.3B ceiling IDIQ for 19 missions (~$279M/mission average, but a ceiling, not a firm per-mission price). Bruno has publicly targeted future commercial Vulcan pricing 'as low as $100 million.' Launches paused for NSSL missions since a Feb 12 2026 USSF-87 SRB nozzle anomaly (the second such SRB issue after Cert-2 in Oct 2024); status as of this research (July 2026) is paused pending investigation.

capex_program_basis: REAL, on-the-record statement by Rocket Lab founder/CEO Peter Beck (Oct 2020): 'It took us $100m to get to orbit and I believe that was too much!' Widely cited secondary compilation (Payload Research) lists this as $100M nominal / $123M inflation-adjusted. No more precise SEC-filed figure exists because Rocket Lab did not go public (NASDAQ: RKLB) until 2021, after Electron was already operational, so pre-IPO development capex was never itemized in a 10-K.
capex_first_launch_basis: Same Peter Beck 'less than $100M on development' statement, referring to spend through the vehicle's path to first orbital flight (May 2017); Beck separately cited $180M as TOTAL spend as of Oct 2020 (including 3 launch pads, production facilities, 2 mission controls, and 14 flights by then) -- that $180M covers post-first-flight scale-up, not just development-to-first-launch, so not used here.
payload_leo_note: Standard payload to LEO as of the Aug 2020 performance upgrade (up from an original 225 kg at debut); ~200 kg to SSO. Booster recovery (helicopter mid-air catch / ocean splashdown, for Rutherford engine reuse) does not meaningfully reduce quoted payload.
opex_per_kg_basis: REAL SEC-disclosed marginal cost (Q1 2025 10-Q) / rated LEO capacity
notes: THE STRONGEST REAL-DATA POINT IN THE NEW-SPACE COHORT: opex_marginal_usd of $5.675M is a REAL SEC-disclosed figure -- Rocket Lab's Form 10-Q for Q1 2025 breaks out the Launch Services segment as $35.592M revenue / $28.375M cost of revenue / $7.217M gross profit across 5 confirmed Electron missions that quarter, giving average revenue/launch of $7.12M and average MARGINAL COST/launch of $5.68M -- an actual disclosed operating-cost data point, not an estimate. opex_price reflects Rocket Lab's own Q1 2026 earnings-call disclosure that new commercial Electron missions in backlog are priced ~$8.5M, up from $5-6M at 2018 market entry and $7.5M for years prior to 2023 (Q3 2024 new-contract ASP was $8.4M, a 67% increase since debut, per investor materials). num_flights=91 orbital launches (87 success/4 failure, ~95.6%) plus 9 separate suborbital HASTE missions (not counted), as of late June 2026. Most-flown new-space small launcher in history; publicly traded (NASDAQ: RKLB).

capex_program_basis: No official CASC/Chinese state figure for CZ-3B development cost has ever been disclosed; genuine data gap after searching Cox Report chapters, CRS reports, and Chinese state media.
capex_first_launch_basis: Same gap as total program cost.
payload_leo_note: CZ-3B is almost never flown to LEO commercially; its real market is GTO (5,100-5,500 kg for the 3B/E variant). $/kg below uses the LEO rated capacity per this dataset's standard convention, but commercial pricing actually applies to GTO missions (effective ~$12,700-13,700/kg-to-GTO at the $70M price point).
opex_per_kg_basis: REAL standing CGWIC commercial rate (2013) / LEO rated capacity (see payload note re: GTO caveat)
notes: THE BEST-DOCUMENTED HISTORICAL COMMERCIAL-PRICING CASE IN THE DATASET. Real 1990s prices, tied to actual US-China trade disputes: $25M offered for Arabsat (1990, triggered Arianespace/US government pushback over 'dumping', per CRS report 98-575); ~$30M for AsiaSat 1 (1990, first Chinese commercial launch for a foreign customer); $56M for Intelsat 708 (1992 contract; the Feb 1996 launch failure destroyed the satellite and killed people on the ground at Xichang). A 1995 US-China bilateral agreement required Chinese prices to stay within 15% of Western prices or trigger a US pricing review; in 1997 USTR found China had violated this on the Agila-2/Loral launch for the Philippines. CGWIC's standing commercial rate was reaffirmed at $70M in 2012-2013 (explicitly backed by a '96% success record over 181 flights' -- a genuine disclosed rate card, used here) and reportedly cut to $50M by 2019 amid SpaceX price competition. ~116 flights, ~96.5% success rate, including a Jan 2026 Shijian-32 failure.

capex_program_basis: No disclosed CASC/state development budget for CZ-5 itself. Only adjacent, non-equivalent figures found: Wenchang launch site infrastructure (~RMB 5bn / $810M) and a CZ-5 production facility (~RMB 4.5bn / $650M) -- these are launch-site/manufacturing capex, not vehicle R&D cost, so not used.
capex_first_launch_basis: Same gap as total program cost.
payload_leo_note: 25,000 kg to LEO is the CZ-5B (core-stage-only) variant, used for space-station module launches; standard CZ-5 carries 14,000 kg to GTO. CZ-5 is primarily a government/state-mission vehicle (space station, lunar sample return, Mars) and is not actively marketed with a disclosed commercial contract price the way 3B/2D are.
opex_per_kg_basis: ESTIMATE (analyst figure, NOT a confirmed real contract price -- see notes) / CZ-5B LEO capacity
notes: UNLIKE CZ-3B/2D, this price is NOT a confirmed real contract: the ~$160M figure is a secondary/analyst estimate (Wikipedia infobox), since CZ-5 has no disclosed CASC/CGWIC commercial contract (it's overwhelmingly a state-mission vehicle). A Sept 2022 CASC report in Aerospace China magazine rated CZ-5/5B in the top cost-competitiveness tier alongside Falcon 9 for their orbit classes but gave no absolute dollar figure. 94.4% success rate over 18 flights (17/18), including the 2017 CZ-5 Y2 core-stage failure that caused a 28-month launch hiatus.

capex_program_basis: No official CASC/Chinese state development-cost figure disclosed; genuine gap despite search.
capex_first_launch_basis: Same gap as total program cost.

opex_per_kg_basis: REAL repeat-customer commercial price / rated LEO capacity
notes: REAL, FLIGHT-PROVEN DATA. China's most-flown active workhorse (100th mission passed in 2025), ~99% success rate over 105 flights. Real, disclosed modern commercial pricing exists via repeat domestic-commercial customer Changguang Satellite Technology (Jilin-1 constellation): 112.9-113 million yuan (~$15.7-16M) per mission reported for 2022-era contracts -- this is a genuine repeat-customer procurement price. capex_program_basis: No disclosed CASIC/ExPace development budget for KZ-1A found despite search.
capex_first_launch_basis: Same gap as total program cost.
payload_leo_note: Payload varies by source/orbit: 200 kg to 700km SSO, 250 kg to 500km SSO, up to 300-400 kg to lower LEO. Using the commonly-cited 300 kg LEO figure.
opex_per_kg_basis: REAL commercial per-launch price / commonly-cited LEO capacity
notes: REAL, FLIGHT-PROVEN DATA. Quasi-commercial CASIC/ExPace solid rocket with genuinely operator-disclosed pricing: ExPace publicly advertised $10,000-$20,000/kg (stated goal of reaching $5,000/kg) starting ~2016; individual missions are commonly listed at $5.8M per complete launch service, consistent with the operator's own per-kg claim at ~300kg payload. 16 dedicated KZ-1A flights through Dec 2024 (14 successes, 2 failures: Sept 2020, Dec 2021; ~87.5% success). An upgraded KZ-1A-Pro variant debuted Dec 2024 and flew several more missions through 2025 (4 Kuaizhou-series missions in 2025: 3 successes, 1 failure) -- combined family total by mid-2026 is approximately 20+ flights, but num_flights here reflects the baseline KZ-1A variant specifically (16) since a fully reconciled combined figure wasn't available from one authoritative source.

status: operational (declared so after June 2025 flight, >decade after debut)
capex_program_basis: Cumulative spending on the Angara rocket family from 1995 development start through 2012, as estimated by then-Roscosmos chief Vladimir Popovkin -- widely cited in Western press as evidence of severe cost/schedule overruns (development began 1995, targeting 2005, didn't fly until Dec 2014). Excludes ~100-150 billion rubles of separate ground infrastructure investment at Plesetsk/Vostochny and the follow-on A5B program.
capex_first_launch_basis: Same Popovkin 2012 estimate; no separate total was disclosed for 2012-2014, but the 2012 figure captures the great majority of development spending before the Dec 2014 first flight.
payload_leo_note: 24,500 kg to 200km/60 deg orbit, per Khrunichev data.
opex_per_kg_basis: government/designer cost disclosure (not a market contract -- no Western commercial customers) / rated LEO capacity
notes: REAL government-disclosed data, though not a market-tested price (Angara has no commercial customers). Salyut Design Bureau general designer Sergey Kuznetsov stated in 2021 costs run 'between $50 million and $100 million,' closer to the upper bound during the current low-rate/experimental production phase. Unit production cost separately reported at 7 billion rubles (2019, vs. Proton-M's ~2.3B rubles), with a goal of cutting to 4-5 billion rubles via serial production. 5 flights through June 2025: 4 successes, 1 partial failure (Dec 2021, upper-stage restart failure stranded payload in LEO). Human-rated Angara-A5M variant (Orel/Oryol crew capsule) not expected before 2028-2031.

capex_program_basis: Total international-consortium investment (Boeing 40%, RSC Energia 25%, Ukraine's Yuzhnoye/Yuzhmash 20%, Norway's Aker 15%) in the Odyssey floating launch platform, Sea Launch Commander assembly/command ship, and launch system, per RussianSpaceWeb; grew from an initial 1996 budget of $583M. Excludes ~$2 billion in liabilities/creditor claims accumulated by the 2009 bankruptcy (debt service/operating losses, not capex).
capex_first_launch_basis: Same total investment figure; platform and ship were complete in time for the March 1999 demonstration flight and October 1999 first commercial flight.
payload_leo_note: Nominal Zenit-3SL LEO capability (~7,000 kg); Sea Launch flew exclusively GTO commercial missions (6,000-6,160 kg) and never operationally used the LEO configuration, so this is a theoretical vehicle spec, not an operational record. On the real, operationally-used GTO basis, effective price is ~$16,667/kg.
opex_per_kg_basis: REAL arm's-length commercial contract (Hughes, Dec 1995) / nominal (untested) LEO capacity
notes: ONE OF THE STRONGEST REAL-MARKET-PRICING CASES IN THE ENTIRE DATASET for a Russian/Ukrainian-heritage vehicle: Hughes Space and Communications' Dec 1995 contract for 10 firm launches at $1 billion total ($100M/launch) was a genuine arm's-length commercial deal, not a government estimate -- the deal that made Sea Launch 'a real business' per its GM at the time. Secondary reporting indicates prices later rose toward $110-120M/launch by the early 2010s as flight rate declined. 36 launches 1999-2014: 32 successes, 3 failures (ICO F-1 2000, NSS-8 2007, Intelsat-27 2013), 1 partial failure (2004). Filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy June 2009 (~$2B in creditor claims, incl. $977.5M Boeing claim), emerged Oct 2010 under 95% Russian (Energia) ownership. S7 Group (Russian airline) bought the assets in 2016 (~$109-150M reported), relocated platform/ship to Vladivostok by 2020, estimated refurbishment cost ~$470M. Dormant since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine severed the Russia-Ukraine cooperation the Ukrainian-built Zenit depends on; a Soyuz-5-based revival has been floated but is unconfirmed.

capex_program_basis: Sum of JAXA Phase 1 (original 3-stage E-X, ~$200M, through 2013 debut) and Phase 2 (Enhanced Epsilon 4-stage upgrade, estimated $100-150M, midpoint used, through 2016 second flight), per JAXA figures reported by SpaceNews.
capex_first_launch_basis: JAXA Phase 1 development budget, covering the original 3-stage E-X Epsilon through its first flight in Sept 2013.
payload_leo_note: 1,200 kg to a 250x500km orbit, standard Enhanced Epsilon config per JAXA's own program page (options: 700 kg to 500km circular LEO, 450 kg SSO).
opex_per_kg_basis: JAXA institutional launch cost (not a commercial market price -- Epsilon primarily launches Japanese government/JAXA payloads) / rated LEO capacity
notes: REAL, FLIGHT-PROVEN DATA (institutional, not commercial-market). First (2013) launch cost ~3.8 billion yen (~$38-44.5M), explicitly targeted at roughly half the ~$70M (7.5 billion yen) cost of the retired M-V solid rocket it replaced; JAXA/IHI planned further cuts to ~3 billion yen/launch with Phase 2 improvements. 6 flights: successes in 2013, 2016, 2018, 2019, 2021; failure Oct 2022 (attitude-control fault, destroyed by flight termination system). Next-generation Epsilon S delayed by a 2023 static-fire test failure, now targeting 2026.

status: development complete, transitioning to commercial production under HAL/NSIL
capex_program_basis: Rs. 169.07 crore total sanctioned cost, per Indian Parliament (Rajya Sabha) written reply by Minister of State Dr. Jitendra Singh, 16 Dec 2021 -- a genuine primary parliamentary source. Covers vehicle development, qualification, and all three developmental flights (D1-D3) collectively; not broken out per flight. Converted at ~INR83/USD.
capex_first_launch_basis: The disclosed Rs. 169.07 crore figure is an all-up sanctioned program cost covering all three developmental flights (through Aug 2024) together; no official breakdown isolating spend through just the first (Aug 2022) flight was found.
payload_leo_note: 500 kg to a 500km planar orbit (35-55 deg inclination), per the same Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha reply; 300 kg to 500km SSO.
opex_per_kg_basis: government/NSIL manufacturing-cost target (not yet a fully disclosed real commercial contract) / rated LEO capacity
notes: Manufacturing/launch cost expected at Rs. 30-35 crore (~$3.6-4.2M), midpoint used above. NSIL has begun real commercialization: it signed BlackSky Global (two ~50kg satellites) as a commercial SSLV customer, and market reporting cites $5-7M/launch as the 2025 commercial rate for sub-500kg payloads, though the specific BlackSky contract price is undisclosed. Flight record: SSLV-D1 (Aug 2022) failed due to a software fault causing an incorrect guidance-mode switch after a sensor anomaly, stranding EOS-02/AzaadiSAT; SSLV-D2 (Feb 2023) and SSLV-D3 (Aug 2024) both succeeded. Declared operational post-D3. In Sept 2025, HAL signed a Rs. 511 crore (~$59M) technology-transfer deal with ISRO/IN-SPACe/NSIL to become SSLV's manufacturer, marketer, and commercial operator, targeting full independent HAL production by 2027.

payload_leo_note: Base Tundra configuration; 350 kg to SSO. An upgraded 'Tundra+' variant targets 1,100 kg to LEO / 850 kg to SSO -- not used here since it's a separate, less-defined future configuration.
opex_per_kg_basis: company-stated PREDICTED target cost per kg (not yet demonstrated -- vehicle has not flown)
notes: PRE-FLIGHT / PREDICTED for all figures -- NordSpace is an early-stage Canadian company (also developing the smaller suborbital Taiga rocket as a technology precursor) targeting Tundra IOC by 2028; no flight has occurred. opex_price_usd of $5M is back-calculated from the company's stated ~$10,000/kg LEO cost target x 500 kg base payload -- NOT a disclosed flat launch price. Two-stage vehicle using a common 'Hadfield engine' (turbopump-fed liquid bipropellant) across a multi-engine first-stage cluster and a single vacuum-optimized second-stage engine. Separately, NordSpace was awarded a much larger CA$715M ($715M) contribution from the Canadian Space Agency's Space Technology Development Program (Nov 2025) for advanced additive-manufacturing capability for liquid rocket propulsion and commercialization of responsive orbital launch vehicles -- this is a broader manufacturing-capability award, not Tundra-specific R&D spend, is likely paid out over many years against milestones rather than already spent, and is NOT included in the capex figure above given the scope mismatch and its unusual scale relative to the company's other (much smaller, $250K-$8.33M) grants. Also holds a $3.2M NGen advanced-manufacturing award and smaller NRC IRAP / DND IDEaS grants, none Tundra-specific. capex_program/capex_first_launch deliberately left BLANK (not just uncertain) after peer comparison: the CA$8.33M DND Phase 1 grant is far below every other vehicle in its payload class (Electron/Firefly Alpha ~$100M, RFA ONE $33M raised and still unflown, even SSLV -- a heavily-subsidized ISRO program reusing existing infrastructure -- needed $20.4M) -- using it as a capex figure would imply an unprecedented and implausible level of cost efficiency for an unflown vehicle, so it is excluded from the capex charts entirely rather than plotted misleadingly. The grant itself is still real and is described for context, just not used as a plotted value.
